heading: What relief exists
lede: These are the doors that exist in U.S. immigration law. You cannot tell someone which one is theirs — that is exactly the line. Knowing they exist is what stops anyone walking away believing there is nothing left to try, and it is why getting to a lawyer quickly matters.

paths.name: Asylum
paths.plain: For someone who fears persecution because of their race, religion, nationality, politics, or the group they belong to.

paths.name: A family petition
paths.plain: A U.S. citizen can petition a spouse, child, parent or sibling. A permanent resident can petition only a spouse or unmarried child. Spouses, minor children and parents of citizens skip the waiting line entirely.

paths.name: An employer petition
paths.plain: Usually requires an employer and a long labor certification process. A few categories let a person petition for themselves.

paths.name: U visa
paths.plain: For a victim of a serious crime who was harmed by it and who helps law enforcement. Requires a certification signed by police or a prosecutor.

paths.name: T visa
paths.plain: For a victim of human trafficking. There is no filing deadline.

paths.name: VAWA
paths.plain: For someone abused by a U.S. citizen or permanent resident spouse, parent, or adult child. They file it themselves, and the abuser is never told.

paths.name: Voluntary departure
paths.plain: Leaving without a removal order on their record, which keeps some future doors open. It has strict deadlines and usually a bond. Nobody should choose this without a lawyer.
